name: Horse chestnut extract

lead: Horse chestnut extract comes from the seed of Aesculus hippocastanum and is standardised to about 20% aescin (escin). It is a traditional herbal remedy for swollen, heavy legs linked to chronic venous insufficiency.

For appearance, the payoff is less swelling and puffiness in the lower legs and a cleaner limb outline. Randomised trials in chronic venous insufficiency report reduced leg volume with the extract, and a 1996 Lancet trial compared it with compression stockings.

paras: It is taken as oral supplements or used in topical gels. People using it for leg puffiness typically combine it with compression and activity, and describe effects over weeks.

Raw horse chestnut seed, leaf, bark and flower are toxic and should not be eaten. The US FDA classifies the seed as an unsafe herb, and processed extracts are used instead. High intravenous aescin doses in cardiac surgery patients have been linked to kidney injury.

chain: Escin supports vein walls and lymph drainage
angle.text: The extract is taken to reduce fluid swelling in the legs, so legs look and feel less puffy. The benefit comes through reducing edema linked to venous insufficiency.

lead: Horse chestnut seed extract comes from Aesculus hippocastanum and is standardised to about 20% aescin, the main active saponin.[1] It is used in traditional and modern herbal medicine for the vein tone and swelling of chronic venous insufficiency (CVI).[1][2]

For appearance, the interest is reduction of leg swelling and heaviness, giving slimmer, less puffy lower legs. Venoactive compounds as a class act by sealing the endothelial barrier, enhancing lymphatic drainage and reducing swelling and inflammation.[3]

Human trials in CVI include a 1996 Lancet comparison of oral horse chestnut seed extract with compression stockings, a comparison with oxerutins measuring leg volume, a study of transcapillary filtration, and a comparison with Pycnogenol.[4][5][6][7] A Cochrane-listed group of compounds called rutosides, which derive from horse chestnut, has also been reviewed for post-thrombotic syndrome.[8][9]

paras: The extract is used for chronic venous insufficiency, where the main outcomes are leg volume and symptoms such as heaviness.[4][7] A 2012 Cochrane review of low-quality studies found seed extract may be an efficacious and safe short-term treatment for CVI, noting that definitive RCTs had not been done.[1]

People use it for puffy, swollen legs. Primary-care guidance on peripheral edema is the wider context for such swelling.[10] A comparison of oxerutins and horse chestnut extract in postmenopausal women used leg volume reduction as its main criterion.[4]

Escin is a triterpenoid saponin mix with anti-inflammatory and anti-edematous properties, and is also being studied in cancer cell models.[11] Bioavailability of beta-aescin has been compared across two formulations in a randomised study.[12]

Raw seed, leaf, bark and flower are toxic because of aesculin and should not be ingested; the FDA classes horse chestnut seed as an unsafe herb. High intravenous aescin doses in cardiac surgery patients were associated with kidney impairment.[1]

A 1996 Lancet trial compared compression stocking therapy with oral horse chestnut seed extract in CVI.[5] A 1986 German trial examined effects on transcapillary filtration.[6] A multicentre comparison with oxerutins in 137 postmenopausal women with CVI measured leg volume, with both agents reducing volume.[4] A trial compared a horse chestnut product with Pycnogenol.[7] A 2025 review of venoactive compounds uses GRADE to place them within chronic venous disease treatment.[3]
